materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 1: Probability and Counting

notes.summary: Joe Blitzstein starts Stat 110 with the two pillars: a sample space (all possible outcomes of an experiment) and counting (how many outcomes have the property you care about). The multiplication rule and the choose function (n choose k) are introduced as the workhorses of the entire course. Everything later — conditioning, expectation, distributions — stands on this combinatorial foundation.
notes.focus: Solve one birthday-style counting problem two ways — direct counting and its complement. The complement trick will save you repeatedly all term.

lessons.title: Story Proofs and the Axioms of Probability

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 2: Story Proofs, Axioms of Probability

notes.summary: Story proofs — counting the same set by two different narratives — prove identities like Vandermonde's convolution without algebra. Then the axioms: nonnegativity, total probability 1, and countable additivity. From three axioms Blitzstein derives inclusion-exclusion and the complements rule, making probability a theorem system rather than folklore.
notes.focus: Prove a binomial identity by story this week. If you can tell a counting story that convinces a skeptic, the algebra will always take care of itself.

lessons.title: The Birthday Problem and Properties of Probability

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 3: Birthday Problem, Properties of Probability

notes.summary: The famous birthday problem: with just 23 people, a shared birthday is more likely than not. The lesson is deeper than the party trick — independence assumptions make exact computation feasible, and 'coincidences' are common because the number of pairs grows quadratically. This lecture cements the probability properties you will use daily.
notes.focus: Redo the birthday calculation for a shared birth MONTH and check it against 23. Generalizing the problem is the fastest way to own the pattern.

notes.summary: Conditioning is the course's superpower: P(A|B) restricts the universe to B and renormalizes. From the definition flow the multiplication rule, the law of total probability, and Bayes' rule — the machinery for updating beliefs with evidence. Medical-test problems (base rates matter!) make the difference between intuition and correctness vivid.
notes.focus: Work a medical screening problem twice — once with natural frequencies (counts out of 10,000), once with Bayes' formula. Frequencies make Bayes feel obvious; that is the point.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 5: Conditioning Continued, Law of Total Probability

notes.summary: Advanced conditioning: partition the sample space, weight by conditionals, and first-step analysis for processes that unfold in stages (gambler's ruin preview). The techniques here convert 'I don't know where to start' problems into 'condition on the first step' recipes — the single most productive habit in this course.
notes.focus: Take one two-stage game and solve it purely by first-step conditioning. Then sanity-check with a brute-force enumeration — both should agree.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 6: Monty Hall, Simpson's Paradox

notes.summary: Two famous paradoxes, both resolved by conditioning carefully. Monty Hall: switching wins 2/3 because Monty's choice is informative, not random. Simpson's: aggregated trends can reverse across subgroups when a confounder is ignored. Both are the same lesson — the data-generating story matters as much as the numbers.
notes.focus: Explain to someone non-technical why switching in Monty Hall wins. If you can do that in under a minute, you truly understand conditioning.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 7: Gambler's Ruin and Random Variables

notes.summary: Gambler's ruin — will a random walk hit the boundary before going broke? — is solved with first-step conditioning and difference equations. Then the course pivots to its central object: the random variable, a numerical function on the sample space. From here on, the subject becomes the study of distributions.
notes.focus: Derive the gambler's ruin probability for a fair coin yourself using first-step analysis. It is the template for Markov-chain problems in CS188 later in your path.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 8: Random Variables and Their Distributions

notes.summary: Distributions describe what a random variable does: the PMF lists P(X = k), the CDF accumulates P(X <= k). You meet the named families — Binomial (fixed trials), Geometric (waiting time), and the story each distribution tells. Choosing the right named distribution is a pattern-matching skill this lecture trains directly.
concepts: CDFs and how to read them
notes.focus: For each named distribution, write its story in one sentence (n trials, k successes...). When you can match problem to story instantly, the formulas follow.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 9: Expectation, Indicator R.V.s, Linearity

notes.summary: Expectation is the long-run average, and linearity of expectation — E(X+Y) = E(X)+E(Y) with NO independence required — is the most useful theorem in the course. The method of indicators decomposes hard problems into 0/1 pieces: count successes by summing 'did this particular event happen' variables. The birthday problem falls to indicators without a single factorial.
notes.focus: Recompute the expected number of matching birthday pairs with indicators only. Then use the same trick on a matching-hats problem — the pattern generalizes.

notes.summary: Expectation techniques stack: LOTUS (E(g(X)) needs no distribution of g), negative binomial waiting times, and the St. Petersburg paradox show the reach of the toolkit. Variance enters as the expected squared deviation — the course's measure of spread — and the shortcut Var(X) = E(X^2) - (E X)^2 makes it computable.
notes.focus: Compute the variance of a die roll by the shortcut formula. Then ask what variance would mean if you played the game 100 times — spread is about experience, not expectation.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 11: The Poisson Distribution

notes.summary: Poisson approximates Binomial when n is huge and p is tiny: rare events over a continuum. Its clean variance-equals-mean property and e^-lambda lambda^k formula make it the default model for counts of emails, typos, and website hits. The approximation theorem connects the two stories elegantly.
notes.focus: Estimate a real-world count problem (typos per page) with Poisson and check the Binomial it approximates. When n is large enough, the numbers are indistinguishable.

materials.videoTitle: Harvard Stat 110 Lecture 12: Discrete vs. Continuous, the Uniform

notes.summary: The bridge lecture doubles as your consolidation checkpoint: continuous random variables replace PMFs with PDFs and sums with integrals, with the Uniform distribution as the first example. Before watching, redo three strategic practices cold — conditioning, indicators, and a named-distribution choice — since the continuous half assumes all of it.
notes.focus: Convert one discrete problem you already solved into its continuous analog (uniform instead of fair die). The translation itself is the lesson.

notes.summary: The normal distribution closes the term: symmetry, the 68-95-99.7 rule, standardization with Z-scores, and the reason the bell curve appears everywhere (the CLT, arriving in the continuation). From counting to conditioning to expectation to continuous families, you now hold the full probabilist's toolkit that 6.006's randomized algorithms and 6.036's ML will silently assume.
notes.focus: Write the course map from memory — counting, conditioning, random variables, expectation, distributions — and place one worked problem next to each node. That map is your final artifact.
